260.title: Dhammas: the hindrances
260.hook: desire present, he knows; absent, he knows; how it arises, how it goes (MN 10)
260.howItsDone: Meditation teachers in a number of Buddhist traditions teach the five hindrances early, so that practitioners can recognize sensual desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness and doubt as passing states rather than personal failures.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was knowing, and your line was just know it: see a mood clearly before changing it. Day two hundred sixty, and the fourth foundation begins.

Sit quietly for five minutes and the usual visitors tend to arrive. First, the snack you suddenly want. Then irritation at the neighbor's leaf blower. Then a heavy, sleepy fog. Then a jittery itch to check your phone. And finally a little voice: is this even doing anything? It's tempting to read them as proof of being bad at meditation. The Buddha named all five, and made knowing them part of the practice. Today: dhammas, the hindrances.
screen: `THE SNACK, THE LEAF BLOWER, THE FOG.` → `IS THIS EVEN WORKING?` → `THE FIVE VISITORS, NAMED.`

segments.voice: The fourth foundation is called dhammas, a hard word here. It can mean teachings, or mental qualities, or the patterns the Buddha taught people to recognize in experience. The first pattern is the five hindrances, the nivaranas, things that cover over a clear mind. Sensual desire. Ill will. Sloth and torpor, that heavy, dull fog. Restlessness and worry. And doubt. For each one, the sutta gives the same five-part instruction. If desire is present in you, know that it's present. If it's absent, know that it's absent. Know how desire that hasn't arisen comes to arise. Know how arisen desire is let go of. And know how, once let go of, it doesn't come back. So the hindrances aren't enemies to fight or proof that you're failing. They're patterns to study. When did the sleepiness come in? Right after lunch. What lifted it? Opening the window. When did the doubt show up? Right when things got boring. You become a naturalist of your own mind, watching creatures arrive and leave. Elsewhere the Buddha compares a mind free of the hindrances to someone out of debt, recovered from illness, released from prison, freed from slavery, and safely across a desert. That's the text's own picture of their going. But the first step is only this: it came, and it went.

segments.voice: Rest with the breath and wait for one of the five visitors: wanting, irritation, dullness, restlessness, or doubt. When one arrives, name it, wanting is here, and notice what it feels like without chasing it away. If you catch the moment it fades, name that too: wanting is gone.
Dhammas, the hindrances. Desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness and doubt: known when present, known when absent, watched as they come and go.
Your line: it came, it went. The visitors aren't failures; they're patterns to study. That's day two hundred sixty.

261.title: Dhammas: the five heaps
261.howItsDone: The five aggregates are taught widely in Buddhist schools; practitioners contemplate them to see that each is changing and that no lasting, controlling self is found among them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhammas, the hindrances. Five visitors, and your line, it came, it went. Day two hundred sixty-one.

Point to yourself. Go ahead. Where did your finger land? Maybe the middle of your chest. But is that you? Your chest is a body part. Your feelings are somewhere else. Your thoughts seem to be up in your head. Your memories aren't anywhere you can point to at all. People say I all day long, and it sounds like one solid thing. The Buddha suggested that if you look closely, what you call I comes apart into five heaps. Today's word: khandha.

Khandha means a heap, a bundle, a mass, like a bundle of sticks. The Buddha taught that what's called a person can be seen as five of them. Form, rupa: the body and the physical world. Feeling, vedana: pleasant, painful, neither, the second foundation. Perception, sanna: recognizing, labeling, that's a cup, that's my friend. Formations, sankhara: intentions, habits, the urges and choices that shape what you do. And consciousness, vinnana: the plain knowing of anything at all. The sutta's instruction for each heap: such is form, such is its arising, such is its passing away. The same for feeling, perception, formations and consciousness. Why sort yourself into heaps? Because in the Buddha's teaching, each heap, looked at closely, is changing all the time, and none of them, on its own, is a solid owner in charge of the rest. That's what the Buddha pointed to with anatta, not-self. As it's usually taught, it isn't a claim that nobody is here. It's that a self of one piece, fixed and in control, isn't found in any of the five. Elsewhere the Buddha gives a picture for each. Form is like a lump of foam on a river. Feeling, a bubble on the water. Perception, a mirage. Formations, the trunk of a banana tree, layer after layer and no hard core. And consciousness, a magician's trick.

Five heaps, one moment. Then let it go, and wait for the next one.
Khandha. A heap: the Buddha's five, form, feeling, perception, formations and consciousness, each one arising and passing.
Your line: five heaps. Sorted into five, one moment can look a little less solid. Day two hundred sixty-one, done.

262.title: Dhammas: the sense bases
262.hook: eye and forms, ear and sounds, and the fetter that arises with them (MN 10)
262.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics and lay practitioners practice 'guarding the sense doors': not avoiding sights and sounds, but noticing the wanting or aversion that arises with them before it takes hold.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was khandha, and your line was five heaps: form, feeling, perception, formations, consciousness. Day two hundred sixty-two.

You're walking past a bakery, not hungry at all. Then the smell reaches you. Ten seconds later you're holding a cinnamon roll and wondering how it happened. Or a certain song comes on, and suddenly you're in a mood about someone you haven't thought of in years. It all started at a door: the nose, the ear. Something came in, and before you noticed, something hooked you. The sutta has a word for that hook. Today: dhammas, the sense bases.
screen: `THE BAKERY SMELL.` → `THE OLD SONG.` → `SOMETHING CAME IN AND HOOKED YOU.`

segments.voice: The sense bases, ayatana, come in six pairs. Eye and forms. Ear and sounds. Nose and smells. Tongue and tastes. Body and touches. And one the Buddhist tradition adds that English usually doesn't: mind and mind-objects, thoughts, memories, ideas, which the mind senses just as the eye senses color. For each pair the instruction is the same. The practitioner knows the eye, knows forms, and knows the fetter that arises dependent on both. Then, like the hindrances: how an unarisen fetter arises, how an arisen fetter is let go of, and how it doesn't come back. A fetter, samyojana, is something that ties you, a knot or a chain. The eye isn't the problem. Neither is the bakery. The fetter is what arises where they meet: the little knot of wanting, or of pushing away, that ties you to what you saw or smelled. Picture each sense as a door of your house. Things will always walk up to the doors; that's life, and it's fine. The practice is to stand at the door and see what comes through with them: this sound came in, and a knot of irritation right behind it. Seen at the door, the fetter is still small. Seen twenty minutes later, you're already holding the cinnamon roll. Elsewhere the Buddha teaches what's called guarding the sense doors, close kin to this. As it's usually explained, it doesn't mean shutting them. It means being home when someone knocks.

segments.voice: Rest at the doors, eyes open or closed, and let a sound come in, then a smell or a touch, then a thought arriving at the mind's door. For each one, check whether a little knot came in too, a like, a dislike. If it did, just see it; seen, it may loosen.
Dhammas, the sense bases. Six doors, eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind, and the fetter that can arise where a sense meets its object.
Your line: the fetter at the door. Six doors, and you can be home at every one. See you tomorrow.

263.title: Dhammas: the factors of awakening
263.hook: mindfulness, investigation, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, equanimity (MN 10)
263.howItsDone: In Theravada countries the Bojjhanga Sutta is chanted as a protective text (paritta), especially for the sick, and meditation teachers use the seven factors to balance a mind that is too dull or too restless.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhammas, the sense bases, six doors. Your line was the fetter at the door. Day two hundred sixty-three.

It's easy to think Buddhist practice is mostly about getting rid of bad stuff: the hindrances that cover a clear mind, the fetters at the doors. The sutta doesn't stop there. Right after them, it names the good stuff: seven qualities that, when they grow together, carry a person to awakening. If the hindrances are weeds, these are the seeds. Today's word: bojjhanga, the factors of awakening.
screen: `NOT ONLY GETTING RID OF THINGS.` → `IF HINDRANCES ARE WEEDS.` → `THESE ARE THE SEEDS.`

segments.voice: Bojjhanga joins bodhi, awakening, and anga, a limb or factor. The sutta lists seven. First, mindfulness, sati, the one this whole sutta is about. Second, investigation of dhammas: looking closely, with curiosity, at what's happening. Third, energy, viriya, the ardent warmth you met a couple of weeks ago. Fourth, joy, piti, a bright, uplifting gladness. Fifth, tranquility, passaddhi, a calming of body and mind. Sixth, concentration, samadhi, a mind gathered and steady. And seventh, equanimity, upekkha, the same balance that ended the immeasurables a few weeks back, here as the last step. The instruction mirrors the hindrances: know a factor present, know it absent, know how it comes to arise, and how, once arisen, it's brought to fullness. And the order flows. Mindfulness notices; investigation gets curious; curiosity wakes up energy; energy brightens into joy; joy settles into tranquility; tranquility gathers into concentration; and concentration rests in equanimity. Teachers often say the first three lift a sluggish mind and the last three calm a restless one, with mindfulness useful at every moment. The seven are also chanted. In Theravada countries they're recited for the sick, because a sutta tells of the Buddha reciting them to a monk who was ill, and the monk recovering. People still chant them at hospital bedsides today.

segments.voice: Recite the seven slowly, one per breath, and check each one: mindfulness, investigation, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, equanimity. Is it here, even a flicker, or is it absent? Present or absent, just know it; then say all seven again, and rest.
Bojjhanga. The seven factors of awakening, from mindfulness to equanimity, each one flowing into the next.
Your line: seven factors. Seven qualities to grow, each one leading into the next. Until tomorrow.

264.title: Dhammas: the four truths
264.hook: he knows as it really is: this is dukkha, its arising, its ceasing, the way (MN 10)
264.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often present the four noble truths in the pattern of a physician's diagnosis, and in insight meditation they are contemplated directly in experience rather than only studied as doctrine.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was bojjhanga, and your line was seven factors: mindfulness, investigation, energy, joy, tranquility, concentration, equanimity. Day two hundred sixty-four.

A good doctor does four things, usually in this order. What's wrong? What's causing it? Can it get better? What's the treatment? Skip a step and things go badly. Treat the symptom without the cause, and it comes back. Believe it can't get better, and you won't try. Teachers often point out that the Buddha's first teaching has this same shape. And the Satipatthana Sutta, after everything else, ends its tour of the four foundations right back at that first teaching. Today: dhammas, the four truths.
screen: `WHAT'S WRONG? WHAT'S CAUSING IT?` → `CAN IT GET BETTER? WHAT'S THE TREATMENT?` → `THE SHAPE OF THE FIRST TEACHING.`

segments.voice: You met the four noble truths long ago on this path. Here, the sutta turns them into something to watch, not only a teaching to hold. The practitioner knows, as it really is: this is dukkha, the unsatisfactoriness, the stress and pain of life. This is the arising of dukkha. This is the ceasing of dukkha. This is the way leading to its ceasing. As it really is, in Pali yathabhutam, is the key phrase: seeing things the way they are, not the way you're afraid they are or wish they were. Notice where the truths come: at the very end of the fourth foundation, after the body, feelings, mind, the hindrances, the heaps, the sense bases, and the factors of awakening. As if all that watching was training the eyes to see the biggest pattern of all, right inside ordinary experience. A tight chest before a meeting: this is dukkha. Wanting it to go perfectly: that's its arising. The moment you let go of needing it perfect, and the chest loosens: that's its ceasing, even if only for a moment. And the whole practice you've been learning, the breath, the knowing, the kindness: that's the way. The longer version of the sutta, in the Long Discourses, spells each truth out at length. The shorter one keeps it to four plain lines. Either way, the instruction is the same: know it, as it is.
screen: `THE FOUR TRUTHS, WATCHED, NOT ONLY BELIEVED.` · `YATHABHUTAM: AS IT REALLY IS.` · `THE BIGGEST PATTERN, SEEN LAST.` · `A TIGHT CHEST IN FOUR STEPS.` · then, large: `KNOW IT AS IT IS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small problem, not the biggest one, and walk it through four steps: what the discomfort is, plainly; what wanting, or not-wanting, is feeding it; what it would feel like, even for a breath, for that wanting to relax; and what one small, wise step you could take. Then let the problem go, and rest with the breath.
Dhammas, the four truths. Dukkha, its arising, its ceasing, and the way: known, as it really is, inside ordinary experience.
Your line: know it as it is. The biggest pattern, seen in the smallest moments. Day two hundred sixty-four, done.

screen: `DAY 264 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SEVEN YEARS, OR SEVEN DAYS.`

265.title: Seven years, or seven days
265.hook: the promise: practice this way for seven years, or even seven days, and fruit comes (MN 10)
265.howItsDone: Insight meditation retreats in the Theravada world are often run as intensive practice for a set number of days, and some teachers cite the sutta's 'seven days' as encouragement.

segments.voice: Yesterday: dhammas, the four truths. Your line was know it as it is. Day two hundred sixty-five.

Gyms make promises. So do language apps and self-help books. Thirty days to a new you. Fluent in three months. It's easy to get cynical about promises. So it's interesting that this old sutta, after all its careful instructions, ends with a promise of its own. And the way it makes it is strange: it starts big and keeps getting smaller, lowering the bar on purpose. Today: seven years, or seven days.
screen: `THIRTY DAYS TO A NEW YOU.` → `THE SUTTA'S OWN PROMISE.` → `STARTING BIG, GETTING SMALLER.`

segments.voice: Here's how the Satipatthana Sutta ends. The Buddha says that if anyone should develop these four foundations in this way for seven years, one of two fruits can be expected. Either final knowledge, awakening, here and now. Or, if some trace of clinging is left, the stage the tradition calls non-return. Then he stops himself. Never mind seven years. Six years. Five. Four, three, two, one. Never mind a year: seven months. Six months, down to one month, half a month. Never mind half a month. If anyone should develop these four foundations for seven days, one of these two fruits can be expected. And then the sutta closes the circle with its opening line: this is the direct path, for the purification of beings. What do you do with a promise like that? The tradition takes it seriously, and also knows the fruit depends on how deeply one practices, not only on the calendar. The traditional commentary explains that the shorter times apply to people whose practice is already ripe. But any listener can take something from the countdown. It's an invitation, not a threat. The Buddha doesn't say, this will take your whole life, so don't bother starting. He keeps lowering the bar until a person could actually step over it. Seven days is not a lifetime. It's a week. You've already done more than thirty-seven of them on this path.
screen: `SEVEN YEARS: ONE OF TWO FRUITS.` · `SIX, FIVE, FOUR, DOWN TO SEVEN DAYS.` · `BACK TO THE DIRECT PATH.` · `A LOWERED BAR IS AN INVITATION.` · then, large: `EVEN SEVEN DAYS.`

segments.voice: Rest with the breath for a moment. Then, if you'd like, pick one thing from these weeks, knowing the breath, naming your posture, catching the second arrow, naming a hindrance, and promise quietly: for seven days, I'll try this. Let the promise settle, and simply sit with whatever is here.
Seven years. The sutta's closing promise: seven years, then fewer and fewer, down to even seven days of this practice, and fruit can be expected.
Your line: even seven days. The bar is low on purpose. That's day two hundred sixty-five.

266.title: Your four foundations
266.hook: a sitting that moves through body, feeling, mind and dhammas
266.howItsDone: Many practitioners do a sitting that moves through body, feelings, mind and dhammas in turn, and on retreats in the Theravada and insight traditions all four are practiced throughout the day, in sitting, walking and daily tasks.

segments.voice: Yesterday: seven years, or seven days. Your line was even seven days. Day two hundred sixty-six, the last day in the Satipatthana Sutta.

Nothing new to learn today. For three weeks, the Satipatthana Sutta, the discourse on the foundations of mindfulness, came one section at a time: the breath, the postures, the bag of grain, the charnel ground, the second arrow, the five visitors, the six doors, the seven factors. Today it comes together the way it was meant to be used: not as a list, but as one sitting. Today: your four foundations.
screen: `THREE WEEKS IN ONE TEXT.` → `NOTHING NEW TODAY.` → `ONE SITTING, ALL FOUR.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole sutta in one breath. Satipatthana: one way, four doors. The refrain: ardent and gentle. First foundation, the body. Knowing the breath, like the turner at the lathe. The chorus: it arises, it passes. The postures: I know I'm sitting. Clear knowing: even this. The parts: a bag of grain. The elements: four elements. The charnel ground: this body too. Second foundation, feelings: pleasant, painful, neither, and one arrow, not two. Third foundation, the mind: know the mind, and just know it. Fourth foundation, dhammas: the hindrances, it came, it went; five heaps; the fetter at the door; seven factors; and the four truths, know it as it is. And the promise: even seven days. It sounds like a lot. But one way teachers read the order is from the most solid to the most subtle. The body is easy to find: you can always feel your seat. Feelings are quicker, a flicker of pleasant or painful. The mind is subtler again, its whole weather. And dhammas are the patterns running through all of it. Each one is a place to stand. On a scattered day, you might only manage the first. On a clear day, you might move through all four. In another sutta, the Buddha calls the four a person's own home ground: a quail caught by a hawk out in the open field is safe again among the clods of its own ploughed field. The practice isn't to master all four at once. It's to know that wherever you are, one of them is right under your feet.
screen: `THE WHOLE SUTTA IN ONE BREATH.` · `BODY, FEELINGS, MIND, DHAMMAS.` · `FROM MOST SOLID TO MOST SUBTLE.` · `ONE IS ALWAYS UNDER YOUR FEET.` · then, large: `FOUR PLACES TO STAND.`

segments.voice: Take about thirty seconds for each foundation: the body, the breath and the shape of your posture; feelings, what's pleasant, unpleasant or neither; the mind, tight or open, scattered or gathered; dhammas, a hindrance here, or a factor of awakening, a little calm, a little curiosity. Then rest wherever you find yourself. The full version runs fifteen minutes, for any quiet morning you have.
Satipatthana, the foundations of mindfulness: one way and four doors, covering the body, feelings, the mind and dhammas, held together in a single sitting.
Your line: four places to stand. Tomorrow a new part begins: the Heart Sutra. Three weeks in one sutta, done.

what a scholar hears: the 'solid to subtle' order is a teachers' reading, not the sutta's; the Satipaṭṭhāna Saṃyutta (SN 47) collects many shorter suttas on the four, and SN 47.6 calls them a monk's own ancestral territory.

chat.says: Four foundations sounds like a lot. Do I have to do all of them every time?
options: No. Each is a place to stand; on a scattered day, the body alone is enough.
Yes, skip one and the sitting doesn't count; all four, every time.
Only the last one matters; the body is too basic once you've learned the rest.
chat.meaning: Each foundation is a place to stand. Like the quail safe in its own field, one of them is always right under your feet.
